Chapter 4 Engaging AI in emergency medicine for better patient care

Abstract

As artificial intelligence (AI) has enhanced and grown, individuals are interested in discovering how it can be utilized in healthcare. Researchers are currently looking into how machine learning (ML) technologies could be used to make emergency medicine better. People are becoming more and more interested in emerging medicine because it uses AI and ML in a lot of different ways. A lot of progress has been made in the study of AI in the last few years. This is mostly because of how well modern ML methods like deep learning work, how easy it is to get to big datasets, and how fast computers are getting faster. Medical professionals can do more and more tasks that are as good as or better than what doctors can do. In other words, AI is getting better at helping people get better health. AI could be useful in many areas of the emergency department (ED) including the operating room, running the ED, images, keeping track of patients, and making clinical predictions. These different ways show that AI can be used to make EDs better in many ways. Many scientists believe that over the next few years, AI will be used in medicine more and more.

Keywords: Emergency department, artificial intelligence, deep learning, patient care, emergency operation,

4.1 Introduction

Healthcare has used artificial intelligence (AI) for a very long time [1]. Also known as AI, this subject has been an important part of computer science for over 60 years. A subject called medical history, on the other hand, has roots that go back thousands of years. Medicine researchers and AI experts have been working together to find new ways to improve care for patients and make healthcare systems run more smoothly [2, 3]. There are two main types of partnerships between the two fields: those that are driven by technology and those that are driven by problems. When it comes to technology-based study, the main focus is on making and testing new AI algorithms that are meant to solve specific therapeutic problems. The main goal of these algorithms is to be flexible, not to prioritize optimization for handling real-world problems. AI algorithms are tailored to successfully address specific clinical issues within the framework of problem-driven research, resulting in the most effective solutions. Nevertheless, it is crucial to acknowledge that these customized algorithms may not exhibit a high degree of generalizability to other problem domains. The gap between technology-driven and problem-driven study has been narrowing over the past few years.

In the field of medicine, the development of AI has been greatly helped by the creation of an effective information technology system. More and more computers and storage space have made it easier to use advanced AI algorithms to handle huge amounts of healthcare data. Full picture analysis and fast processing of real-time patient monitoring data have been put into place and are now working well. These days, using powerful graphics processing units has made many types of computing much better including deep learning (DL) [4]. These methods are now widely known and used to effectively look at complicated clinical data like medical images [5, 6] and electronic health records (EHRs) [7]. Throughout history, AI technologies have been widely known and used in the fields of intensive care [8] and heart [9]. Researchers have written an in-depth analysis of the latest progress in AI in the medical field as well as predictions about where it might go in the future [10]. Still, because both medicine and AI are very broad fields, it is not possible to give a complete list of all the progress being made at the intersection of AI and medicine.

4.2 What is AI?

During the 1950s, the phrase “artificial intelligence” was introduced by Professor John McCarthy of Stanford University, who defined it as the field encompassing the scientific and engineering principles behind the creation of intelligent computers. AI makes it easier for machines to copy human cognitive skills like learning and solving problems. Machine learning (ML) is a branch of AI that focuses on using data to create computer systems that can learn new things and get better at what they do without being explicitly programmed [11]. Statistical techniques and algorithms are utilized to detect patterns and establish correlations within datasets, hence enabling the development of predictive or decision-making models. The three primary categories into which ML algorithms can be classified are supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning. According to SML, supervised ML uses labeled data to learn about the connection between input factors and a result variable like a positive or negative diagnostic. Development of an SML entails utilization of three distinct datasets. The method initially undergoes a learning process on the training dataset, wherein it iteratively adjusts the weights to minimize a loss function. The loss function is responsible for quantifying the discrepancy between the predicted and observed results for a specific data point. Utilizing a test set, small changes are made to the model parameters to get the best outcomes after the model has been created. A validation set is needed to find overfitting, which is when there is a big difference in how well the model does in learning from the validation set compared to the training set. In essence, the purpose of utilizing a test set is to evaluate the model’s capacity to apply its obtained knowledge to new data.

Unsupervised learning, on the other hand, includes methods that use unlabeled data to find natural trends or groups. The purpose of looking at these groups is to find data points that are alike and those that are different as well as to learn how the data is separated in the feature space. Reinforcement learning lets computers learn how to reach their goals in a social setting by making mistakes and fixing them over and over again. Reinforcement learning works by using rewards or penalties as feedback based on what the agent does, while supervised learning focuses on having labeled data to give feedback to the model. Over a temporal duration, the agent assimilates information on sequences of actions that maximize the cumulative result.

In recent years, the healthcare industry has recognized and expanded its use of DL, a subfield of ML. This can be attributed to its remarkable achievements in effectively addressing a wide range of intricate categorization issues [12]. The aforementioned phenomenon can be partially ascribed to advancements in computer capacity and the availability of increasingly vast quantities of data. Neural network architecture and function are based on the cerebral cortex anatomy and function; this is the foundation of DL algorithms. The neural network architecture consists of interconnected nodes organized in layers, resembling neurons (refer to Figure 4.1). As part of forward propagation, the input data is sent to an input layer and then through a network of hidden nodes that are all linked to each other and have different weights assigned to them. The computation of the input to each node involves taking the weighted total of the outputs from the previous layer. This computed input then undergoes a nonlinear modification to generate the output of the node. The difference between the expected value from the output layer and the ground truth value is measured by the loss function. Backpropagation is an optimization technique that uses the prediction error to change the weights over and over again in order to learn more about the structure of the training data. This makes the model more accurate over time.

4.3 Difference between ML and DL

A basic differentiation between ML and DL techniques may be observed in their distinct learning processes. DL algorithms could independently acquire feature hierarchies, which set them apart from traditional ML approaches that need manual extraction and programming of features. Furthermore, DL frequently necessitates a substantial amount of data in order to make correct predictions, whereas conventional ML techniques may reach a point when the performance of the model no longer improves in proportion to the quantity of data. Another significant distinction between the two methodologies lies in their respective execution times. The training process of DL methods sometimes necessitates a significant duration of time due to the vast number of parameters that must be acquired. DL methods typically need a substantial amount of matrix multiplication operations, leading to a significant reliance on high-performance computing systems.

4.4 Machine learning algorithms in clinical research

The decision tree is a well-known ML model that is used in clinical study and is easy to understand. A guided learning method called the decision tree is organized in a way that looks like a flowchart. The system can do both jobs related to classification and tasks related to regression. The study’s goal was to create a prediction model that can correctly guess the target variable for future events. This was done with the help of a set of rules for making decisions. Utilizing a recursive approach, the method divided the data into subsets, or decision nodes by checking the feature value that leads to the greatest reduction in disorder within the created subsets [13]. There is only one “pure” node if all of its data points belong to the same class in the graph. When a node exhibits an identical distribution of percentages for each class, it results in the highest level of impurity. Figure 4.2 depicts an exemplar decision tree employed in the context of predicting medication dosage. The initial division is predicated upon the body mass index (BMI), suggesting that BMI serves as the most reliable indicator for determining the appropriate dosage amount. Class membership probabilities are assigned to each data point in the final subsets, also known as leaf nodes.

Ensemble learning is a ML method that combines many techniques to make predictions more accurate and less variable. A common ensemble model is the random forest, which takes the predictions of many decision trees and puts them together to make a single forecast. Generally, it is often observed that ensembles possess more predictive capability compared to their individual parts. Linear regression, k-nearest neighbors, support vector machines, naive Bayes, and a number of ensemble methods, such as gradient and adaptive boosting, are also commonly used in the field.

Researchers are very interested in the convolutional neural network (CNN) because it works so well in computer vision applications. This makes it a major step forward in the area of DL. Additionally, a CNN is a specialized type of a DNN that can obtain features in a flexible way by using backpropagation, which eliminates the need for human feature extraction. Over the past few years, several studies have shown that DL can be useful for medical imaging tasks [14]. Researchers have used a CNN to categorize brain tumors into different types, figure out what causes COVID from chest X-rays, and spot diabetic retinopathy [15]. Doctors support neural networks a lot because they can learn feature sets on their own, which is easier now that more advanced DL models have been made. CNN have demonstrated their ability to surpass the constraints of traditional ML models in specific categorization tasks.

The subject of natural language processing (NLP), which focuses on developing machines that can comprehend and analyze human language, has been greatly affected by the advancements in DL [16]. EHRs hold a lot of written information. One way to make good use of all that information is to use NLP in emergency care. A lot of different neural networks have been carefully designed to get useful data from unstructured text data like medical reports and doctor’s notes that are kept in electronic medical records [17, 18]. Using NLP on medical data has shown promise for many medical uses like finding cases of sepsis, appendicitis, and flu [19, 20, 21, 22]. A lot of focus has been paid to recurrent neural networks, CNN, and deep generative models in NLP when it comes to DL. Additionally, it has been utilized in NLP to employ both independent learning and reinforcement learning.

In the area of predictive research, supervised ML algorithms have quickly taken the place of older methods. These algorithms are used to predict the probability of consequences by looking at patient factors that are set up before these events happen. The adaptability of these models makes it possible to find links between attributes (predictors) and results. This should lead to better prediction performance than with basic scoring systems. In conjunction with the conventional application of predictive analyses, causal inference studies have implemented supervised ML algorithms to look into the influence of interventions on desired outcomes. Models are commonly used in observational study for estimating treatment effects, which is necessary for inferring causal links. With the implementation of sophisticated ML models, it is plausible to anticipate a decrease in bias.

4.5 Role of AI in emergency medicine

4.5.1 Role in triage and disposition

Triage is a structured procedure that is implemented in the ED to evaluate patients upon their arrival and assign them a priority based on the severity and urgency of their medical conditions. In normal practice, a triage nurse evaluates patients using vital signs, demographic information, and prescribed diagnostic methods. For someone to become a master in triage, they need to put in a lot of time and practice. Emergency severity index level 3 is frequently selected as the default option when situations occur where immediate, life-threatening problems cannot be identified. On the other hand, this choice could mean that a lot of patients have to wait a long time before they can get medical help and an assessment [23]. When used in the ED, ML models could make the triage process better by making it more accurate and faster. Computer programs that learn from data that the triage staff collects every day can be used to make this change. Aside from being able to predict how bad medical problems will be, ML techniques can also be used to make screening tools that can predict disease-specific weaknesses.

4.5.2 Role in ED operations

A hospital ED needs to plan its resources and keep an eye on its patients all the time. Sun et al. [24] used the autoregressive integrated moving average method to look at time series data and make models that could predict how busy the ED would be. The study shows that predicting models can help with planning and making the best use of staffing resources in the real world. The researchers [25] looked into the problem of overcrowding in EDs by looking at what happens when different plans for staffing doctors are made. To do this, they made a simulation tool built on agents. This tool’s usefulness has been tested in a single hospital ED.

Diagnose-choice tools are very important in ED because they make screening and categorizing patients easier. In their research, the researchers [26] introduced a diagnostic modeling system that has the capacity to automate the development of diagnostic decision support systems. The system was tested in the ED, and it appeared to be scalable enough to be used in other areas. In the same way, researchers [27] used data mining methods to help doctors make diagnoses in a pediatric ED.

AI and ML techniques have been utilized for several operational functions inside the ED. Researchers [28] did a study where they used different data mining methods, like the naive Bayes and C4.5 algorithms, to determine the seriousness of ED patients so that they could be sent to the right room. In a similar manner, researchers [29] used a lot of ML techniques to guess how people with asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD) would feel so that the triage process could work better. Researchers [30, 31] came up with a way to automatically sort computed tomography (CT) reports for both adult and pediatric patients in the ED. The researchers used a method that involved making mixed systems that combined ML algorithms with NLP methods. It was found that NLP had a big effect in a different study [32]. The researchers used an automated system for ED reports called the subjective, objective, assessment, and plan (SOAP).

4.5.3 Role in emergency department operations and management

It is hard to accurately predict future service needs in ED operations because many of the factors involved are random. Some of these factors are the schedules of patients’ arrivals, the different types of medical care and diagnostic tests they need, and the lengths of time they need these services and tests. The use of AI could greatly improve the way EDs work and how hospitals are run at all stages of patient care, from admission to exit. The use of ML could make EDs run more smoothly by figuring out the best way to use resources based on what each patient needs. This, in turn, can lead to a reduction in expenditures and an improvement in patient outcomes. The problem of overcrowding in EDs is a growing concern within the healthcare sector, which can potentially lead to adverse effects on the provision of high-quality patient care [33]. The application of predictive models in the prediction of ED flow has the capacity to support the creation of staffing models and improve readiness for surge and emergencies. Additionally, other confounding factors contribute to the challenge of estimating ED duration for waiting. ML algorithms, possessing capability to discern patterns within intricate collections of features, hold the potential to generate ED wait times of higher accuracy. On a broader scope, in the event that several hospitals in close proximity provide precise wait time information, patients with low acuity conditions would be able to make a selection for ED services based on both distance to be traveled and duration for waiting.

Not all uses of AI will endure and gain the confidence of medical professionals and patients. According to existing literature, there is a higher likelihood of triage and radiology models being implemented at a faster rate compared to other applications in the context of ED operations [34].

4.5.4 Role in medical imaging

The timely access to radiology interpretation is not always available to the ED practitioner. The prompt and efficient availability of medical imaging results is of utmost importance in the proper detection of fracture in X-rays or a stroke in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, as any delays in diagnosis and treatment could potentially lead to misdiagnosis and hindered medical interventions. This aspect becomes particularly crucial while operating within a smaller ED that has restricted availability of specialized medical professional. DL models specifically developed for medical imaging exhibit an exceptional capacity to identify critical medical disorders, hence facilitating expedited diagnosis by healthcare professionals. Recent studies have indicated that the quality of AI interpretation is on a level with that of a skilled radiologist [35].

4.5.5 Role in clinical image analysis

The progress made in the field of picture recognition holds significant relevance for several domains within the realm of clinical image analysis. Presence of extensive labeled image databases has made image analysis a highly productive area of research. Applying DL techniques has shown a high level of accuracy in finding pneumonia on chest X-rays and 3D segmentation of subdural hematomas on brain CT, figuring out the probability that it is cerebral aneurysm ruptures and scoring CT scans of people who may have had an acute ischemic stroke. These achievements have been found to be comparable in accuracy to that of stroke specialists [36, 37]. DL has been utilized in the area of brain MRI to differentiate individuals with a first episode psychosis from a control group as well as to forecast their lifetime consumption of alcohol [38, 39]. DL has been employed in the domain of ultrasonography (USG) as well. It has shown a high level of accuracy in finding free fluid in the abdomen on focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) scans, categorizing abdominal USG pictures and automatically analyzing ejection fraction on echocardiography [40, 41]. DL has also helped new technologies get better. For example, a microwave-based scanning model can correctly tell the difference between an ischemic and a hemorrhagic stroke before the patient gets to the hospital [42].

4.5.6 Role in predictive modeling

Predictive modeling stands as a prominent and inherent use of AI within the domain of medicine. A multitude of AI systems has been created with the purpose of forecasting the likelihood of sickness and its consequences. Significantly, within the field of emergency medicine, there has been extensive exploration of AI in development of prediction models. In their study, researchers [43] employed AI techniques and data mining tools to forecast the admission to the hospital. The researchers [44] employed patient data collected in the ED and employed decision trees, logistic regression, and gradient-boosted machines as components of their methodology. In their study, researchers made a web-based tool that uses a number of data mining and ML methods to instantly figure out the likelihood of someone needing to go to the ED again. The study showed that it is possible to do population-based risk assessment better by combining data from outpatient centers with data from hospitals or EDs. Smart computers, or AI, play a big role in this process. The researchers also made a clinical decision tool that tells how likely it is that a patient will need to go back to the ED in the next 72 h [45]. The tool lets the ED staff and managers use patient-specific data to figure out how likely it is that a patient will return to the ED within 72 h. This could give them more power. This is a chance to give more information and improve patient care so that fewer people have to go back to the ED.

The artificial neural network is one of the most useful and well-known of the many AI tools. One study [46] showed that groups of artificial neural networks can be used to guess how babies and kids with bronchiolitis will be treated in the ED. Nevertheless, it was determined that the accuracy of the stay prediction was low. The researchers [47] used methods from artificial neural networks to make a model that can tell when the craniocervical joint will become damaged in a trauma patient. A study [48] was done that used artificial neural network technology and clinical data gathered during the initial evaluation of patients at the ED to create a predictive model for acute coronary syndromes. In their study, researchers [49] conducted an assessment of the prediction of mortality and acute morbidity using routinely collected variables. This assessment involved the construction of models utilizing a total of 17 statistical and AI methodologies including the implementation of neural networks. A study [50] used artificial neural networks and genetic algorithms, a metaheuristic approach inspired by natural selection, to predict renal colic in emergency medical settings.

Utilization of extensive and intricate datasets for predictive modeling is made possible by the vast quantity of data accessible through EHRs. It is not possible to use classical logistic regression when there are too many independent factors compared to observations. In order to tackle this matter, the utilization of variable selection proves to be both successful and efficient. The researchers [51] did a study in which they came up with a ranking method to find a subset of variables that might be able to predict as well as the whole series of variables. The objective was to evaluate the probability of serious cardiovascular events in ED patients who presented with chest pain. In a study, researchers employed a well-established random forest algorithm to assess the relative relevance of factors and showcased the effectiveness of AI and ML techniques in forcasting in-patient mortality for ED sepsis patients, surpassing the predictive capabilities of clinical scores [52].

4.5.7 Role in clinical monitoring

The implementation of AI-based clinical monitoring systems has the potential to facilitate the timely detection of patients experiencing a decline in their health status. The compensatory reserve index (CRI) uses a number of ML methods to find small changes in the arterial blood pressure (BP) pattern of a finger in order to predict the development of cardiovascular disease in the future [53]. The CRI exhibits a linear reduction after voluntary bleeding. Furthermore, the inclusion of CRI on the monitor screen has been linked to the early detection of imminent instability [54, 55]. A ML model has been developed and trained to evaluate vital signs and detect instances of cardiovascular instability in patients transitioning from the intensive care unit to step down units. On average, this model provides alerts approximately 17 min and 51 s prior to the occurrence of a cardiovascular instability event [56].

The timely identification and intervention of sepsis lead to substantial enhancements in patient outcomes. When applied to the study of changing heart rate and BP, ML algorithms have shown that they can independently identify the onset of sepsis up to 4 h before the first clinical symptoms show up [57]. In a similar vein, InSight is a precise ML-based system for predicting sepsis. It demonstrates resilience in the face of missing data and leverages the temporal evolution of vital signs to effectively forecast the occurrence of sepsis and severe sepsis many hours in advance [58]. The utilization of a DL system to the analysis of electrocardiogram (ECG) data has demonstrated superior accuracy in detecting 15 distinct arrhythmias, sinus rhythm, and noise, surpassing the performance of individual cardiologists [59].

The problem of false alarms, which is now prevalent in “intelligent” monitors, poses a challenge for any system aiming to provide alerts. Back in 2015, there was a worldwide study competition whose main goal was to find ways to use ML to reduce the number of false alarms in critical care units. Plesinger et al. [60] found that the successful model had an 80% success rate in removing fake alarms while only 1% success rate in removing real alarms. It is anticipated that forthcoming monitoring devices would exhibit reduced bulkiness in comparison to existing systems. New methods for measuring heart rate and breathing rate have been created using ML techniques made possible by recent advances in technology. These methods are the only ones that can correctly measure these physiological parameters through video analysis alone, without having to touch the patient directly [61]. ML has been used to learn how to use a single arm band to measure BP without a cuff. Additionally, ML has been employed to effectively forecast BP by utilizing ECG recordings [62, 63].

4.5.8 Role in patient monitoring

With the advent of modern sensor technologies and the increasing computational capabilities, the continuous collection and analysis of extensive physiological data from patients is no longer a mere concept. The researchers [64] presented a comprehensive wireless network that was specifically developed to monitor unchecked individuals in the ED. The study included trying a prototype for a scalable medical alert response technology (SMART) system for the first time. The system was then put into use on a small scale. The authors of a recent study conducted by researchers [65] created and validated an integrated patient monitoring system inside a large-scale ED setting. The system was connected to a peer-to-peer network that had monitors at the bedsides and handheld PDAs. The researchers performed a comparative analysis on two early warning systems, one utilizing an integrated system and the other employing a traditional manual technique. The aforementioned extensive clinical research also examined automated approaches for evaluating patients using EHRs enhanced with AI methodologies. Typically, the integration of patient monitoring systems with AI components is a prevalent practice aimed at enhancing assistive decision-making processes. Earlier research has looked at how AI can be used to manage physiological data, especially electrocardiography, in emergency medical situations [66, 67].

4.5.9 Role in home monitoring of patient

In the future, it is plausible that patients will arrive to the ED at an earlier stage due to the influence of algorithms, and they will possess a greater amount of information. ML has been used to look at telemonitored breathing sounds in order to predict sudden worsenings of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. This approach successfully identified 75.8% of exacerbations in advance, on average 5 days prior to the patient seeking medical assistance [68]. In the same way, earlier research has shown that a ML model might be able to predict when asthma control will get worse in children, up to 1 week before the first noticeable symptoms show up [69]. Wrist-worn accelerometers possess the capacity to identify seizures, whereas “smart carpets” employ floor-based detection systems and utilize ML or smartphone audio systems to determine instances of falls among the elderly [70, 71].

4.5.10 Role in causal inference, risk, prediction, and metrics

According to researchers, there are three main types of data science methods used in medical and epidemiological study. These are description, prediction, and causal inference (also called counterfactual prediction) [72]. Despite the significance of descriptive and predictive studies in comprehending the occurrence, causes, and prognosis of diseases or maladies, physicians generally find it insufficient to rely solely on these research methodologies when attempting to enhance patient outcomes for interventions. Causal inference is a research methodology that attracts considerable attention in the world of medical research. It includes comparing hypothetical prospective outcomes by applying two or more distinct therapies within a certain population.

ML models have the potential to enhance causal inference through many means. Initially, it should be noted that unsupervised learning models possess the capability to discern clusters of patients who exhibit distinct characteristics. According to a recent scholarly work, a comprehensive analysis of data from many observational studies and randomized control trials has revealed the existence of four distinct phenotypes of sepsis that hold clinical significance [73]. The research employed a consensus clustering approach that was based on the k-means algorithm to simplify the classification process. Despite the lack of direct causal inference in this study, the researchers postulated that the phenotypes studied might respond differently to early goal-directed therapy.

Furthermore, it has been observed that supervised learning models have the ability to provide predictions that can identify high-risk patients with greater accuracy compared to previous methodologies. An example of a previously based study used baseline demographic information, chief complaints, vital signs, and patient complications to predict the likelihood of needing critical care, such as being admitted to the intensive care unit or dying in the hospital, as well as the likelihood of being hospitalized for people who come to the ED [74]. The researchers saw that the predictor model using logistic regression did not do as well as the other four ML models (lasso regression, gradient boosting, random forest, and DNN). These models had different levels of accuracy. While the study did not include demonstrating causal linkages, it is worth noting that the early detection of persons at high risk could potentially aid in identifying a particular subgroup that could greatly benefit from timely and intensive interventions.

Finally, ML models could be directly used in causal inference to make a treatment model work better so that a propensity score, an outcome model, or both can be made. It is possible to use more complex methods for this purpose, even though logistic regression is often used to estimate propensity scores. An example of this was a research study that evaluated the effect of transthoracic echocardiography on the mortality rate within 28 days in patients with sepsis in the intensive care unit [75]. The researchers choose to employ gradient boosting, as opposed to logistic regression, as the statistical technique for constructing the treatment model in order to predict propensity scores for the receipt of transthoracic echocardiography. In the same vein, ML models can be implemented to estimate treatment effects in outcome models, thereby simplifying the process of drawing causal inferences.

4.6 Conclusion

Despite certain limits, contemporary AI systems have significant proficiency in effectively addressing clearly defined challenges within a diverse array of therapeutic areas. These devices possess the capability to enhance various facets of emergency patient care. It is quite probable that the capabilities of AI technology will enhance progressively, and the incorporation of these solutions into practical settings holds the potential to yield advantages for patients, physicians, and the general population by facilitating the more effective and precise provision of healthcare services of superior quality.

Chapter 5 Application of AI in ENT (otorhinolaryngology) care

Abstract

The concept of artificial intelligence (AI) has become widely discussed in both popular culture and academic research. In recent years, there have been substantial discussions over its potential to profoundly alter health care delivery. Nevertheless, to now, it has rendered minimal contributions to the domain of medical practice or the enhancement of patient care. The potential integration of AI technologies into the field of otolaryngology may encounter obstacles due to prevailing misconceptions surrounding the nature of AI and concerns over potential machine faults that could impact patient treatment. It is essential for otolaryngologists to have a thorough understanding of AI ideas and implications because of its potential therapeutic and economic benefits. AI is likely to significantly impact biomedical research and the application of medical practices in the near future. Otolaryngologists are crucial contributors to the development and effective application of important AI technologies designed to improve patient care. The acquisition of high-caliber data holds an utmost importance for the advancement of AI technologies. Consequently, otolaryngologists have to actively pursue collaborations with data scientists, with the aim of providing guidance in identifying clinically significant inquiries that can yield substantial impact. AI has significant implications in various domains of otorhinolaryngology. These include the automated diagnosis of hearing loss, the enhancement of hearing aid performance, the restoration of speech in individuals with paralysis, the prediction of speech and language outcomes in candidates for cochlear implants, the diagnosis of various otology conditions through the analysis of otoscopic images, the application of virtual reality simulators for education in otological surgeries, the categorization and measurement of opacification in computed tomography scans of paranasal sinuses, the differentiation of different laryngeal pathologies depending on laryngoscopic images, the automatic segmentation of anatomical structures to expedite radiotherapy planning, and the assistance of pathologists in reporting thyroid cytopathology.

Keywords: Otolaryngology practice, laryngeal pathology, machine learning, artificial intelligence,

5.1 Introduction

The term “computational intelligence,” also referred to as artificial intelligence (AI), encompasses the use of technology to enable computer systems to perform tasks that generally necessitate human intelligence. These activities involve word recognition and identifying objects, visual perception, and intricate decision-making. In the domain of computational learning, algorithms are specifically crafted to collect data from input sources and employ this learned information to generate predictions for unanalyzed data. In medicine, there has been a significant technological shift and a remarkable enhancement in computing capabilities in recent decades [1].

Machine learning (ML) is a domain of AI encompassing a collection of algorithms and methodologies designed to enhance efficiency and precision through the iterative identification of patterns. In ML, computers are trained to recognize patterns in historical data and then apply this learning to forecast the behavior of newly supplied data. There are various classifications of ML. A particular category of ML algorithms is known as artificial neural networks (ANNs). ANNs are engineered to emulate the functional attributes of synapses found in the human brain. ANNs consist of multiple interconnected layers of nodes. Each node performs a sequence of computations based on the inputs and outputs it receives. Furthermore, each node in the network establishes connections with other nodes. Information flows through numerous hidden levels of an ANN, beginning at the input layer and finishing at the output layer. ANNs with multiple hidden layers are commonly termed “deep neural networks.” These networks have been designed to address complex problems, such as voice and picture recognition acquisition [2]. In the domain of ML, commonly referred to as “deep learning (DL),” the algorithm is instructed to identify patterns within extensive datasets [3].

The use of computational intelligence in otorhinolaryngology is still in its early stage, but it offers a lot of promise. The creation of datasets encompassing diverse patient features, disorders, and associated outcomes is a crucial requirement in the domain of AI applications. Considering the patient’s present symptoms, the subsequent step is to recommend particular diagnostic examinations and potential therapeutic interventions. The ML system assesses the precision of its predictions by leveraging its database, therefore guaranteeing that the patient receives the most appropriate treatment.

5.2 Machine learning and deep learning

The area of AI, especially ML and DL, has received a lot of attention from medical professionals and academics since it started in 1990 and 2010. AI, ML, and DL are all strongly linked to each other. It’s not clear what the exact meaning of AI is when it comes to automating jobs that normally need human intelligence [4]. Visual comprehension, object identification and recognition, and making decisions are all part of these tasks. ML and DL are often combined in AI, along with other methods that are hard to use with traditional learning models. ML is an analytical technique that combines concepts from computer science, statistics, optimization, and probability [5]. Several important parts must be present for a ML program to work properly. The following are part of it: (1) the supply of raw data, (2) the availability of accurate prediction instances, and (3) an approach to test and confirm the extent to which the algorithm works. ML uses input data to build a model that shows a clear pattern, which lets people draw rational conclusions [6, 7]. DL is a clear subfield of the larger discipline of ML. DL involves the training of neural networks to acquire a multiplicity of layers, which typically range from tens to hundreds, in order to identify and represent complex patterns and relationships in data. A neural network is a computer model made up of neurons that are all linked to each other. The network can make nonlinear predictions when it is paired with an activation function. On the other hand, traditional ML techniques focus on extracting features, while DL methods use raw data to find good representations for classification [8]. DL has been used in a lot of different AI systems, some of which are meant to be used in medicine [9]. DL can be used for many things, such as organizing pictures into groups, letting cars drive themselves, recognizing speech, and turning text into music. In many situations, studies have shown that DL models work just as well as or better than people. Since ML and DL have made such big steps forward in the medical field, it is very important for doctors to fully understand the pros and cons of data-driven analysis tools.

5.3 Role of AI in audiology

ML advances have caused a big change in the area of auditory sciences. AI-based method makes it easier to diagnose hearing loss by letting auditory brainstem reactions be automatically put into groups and audiometric limits be calculated [10, 11]. In cases where traditional audiometry methods are not available, computational intelligence makes it easier to do hearing tests online. In the study, computational intelligence methods were used to guess how people who were diagnosed with sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) would do with their hearing care [12]. Utilizing online testing, especially for people with SSNHL, can be seen as a practical way to begin treatment in areas on the edges where audiology services are scarce or not available at all. Utilizing AI is essential for making telemapping and troubleshooting for cochlear implants possible, which eliminates the need for people to travel to specialist centers. Furthermore, these services provide individuals with the chance to utilize specialized providers, thereby alleviating the monetary stresses associated with wage loss and transportation expenses [13]. This makes it easier for habilitationists, audiologists, and doctors to do effective follow-ups and urges family members to be involved in rehabilitation programs.

Auditory aid users often complain about how tough it is to understand speech in busy places. This issue is sometimes called the “cocktail party” issue. New advances in AI might be able to help solve this issue. Tracking and evaluating soundscapes is how AI can change the settings of a device based on what the listener wants in different situations. The integration of DL algorithms into the system has the potential to improve the efficacy of AI by increasing the speech-to-noise ratio at the listener’s tympanic membrane. This technological development successfully changes the sound experience from having background noise to having a calm atmosphere. AI can help people with preference listening, especially when they are listening to speakers they do not know or who sound different, by making it easier for them to change their attention. By looking at the listener’s electroencephalogram skills, the goal of the discussion can be reached by decoding the sound input that is meant for the receiver and then sending it as a separate signal. “Source separation” and “cognitive control” are two tools that are used to make this possible. The application of DL-based speech enhancement approaches can lead to improved programming for hearing aid users, resulting in higher satisfaction and increased speech intelligibility [14]. Within the context of those who heavily depend on lip-reading as their major means of communication, the incorporation of digital flashcards and speech-to-text software can prove to be invaluable tools, particularly in the context of the COVID-19 epidemic where face masks are commonly worn by those in their vicinity.

The utilization of DL in advanced AI systems has facilitated the development of methodologies that employ end-to-end decoding, employing neural networks with multiple layers. These systems can immediately convert acoustic waves into text, eliminating the necessity for a hidden Markov model or a distinct language model. This is in contrast to traditional approaches in automatic speech recognition. The application of automatic speech identification and AI allows for the interpretation of spoken language directly from brain cortex activity, resulting in either written output or generated voice waves. With the new developments, researchers have successfully made illustrations of direct neuroprosthesis systems that can read words and sentences right away by observing brain activity. A disease called anarthria makes it hard for people to control their vocal tract while speaking. It can be caused by cerebrovascular accidents or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Such devices are intended to assist people with this disease. Progress in speech neurosciences and AI could help people who are severely paralyzed regain their speaking skills. This would help them avoid the problems that come with natural conversation. Speech and language tests could be made better with AI, which would completely change how children who have hearing loss are restored. Several studies are currently looking into how AI can be used to predict what will happen with speech and language. To do this, brain scans of young children who are getting a cochlear implant can be looked at before the surgery. To achieve this goal, brain imaging techniques like T1 and diffusion tensor imaging scans are used. These are both types of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Following the implantation of a cochlear device, variations in language outcomes may occur among individuals. This is because the auditory system on the outside and the nerve system inside work together. This is because the appropriate functioning of both systems is essential for spoken language. Also, not being able to hear something changes the structure of the brain, which in turn changes the way understand and perceive spoken language. Being able to accurately guess what will happen can help make language therapy and listening training more personalized [15].

5.4 Role of AI in otology

The integration of AI is presently underway in the Otolaryngology-Head & Neck Surgery Department at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Centre in Columbus. Specifically, researchers are focusing on the development of an innovative computer-assisted image processing software known as the “Auto-Scope.” The “Auto-Scope” is a classification system that categorizes tympanic membrane images into two groups: normal and pathological. This intervention has the potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy in primary care settings and mitigate the excessive treatment of ear diseases, thereby contributing to the reduction of antibiotic resistance. AI also contributes to the process of triage and the development of innovative and promising approaches in diagnosing dizziness. Additionally, AI assists in the conventional decision-making process for patients with vertigo [16]. Figure 5.1 presents an illustrative depiction of AI-based mechanism in the understanding of disease on the basis of the data generated with otoscopy, and then the suggestion in the diagnosis and treatment of the disease [17, 18].

5.5 AI-based surgical and training applications in otology

The utilization of the virtual reality simulator, known as “Cardinal Sim,” enables the teaching of temporal bone dissection without the requirement of a human or cadaveric temporal bone specimen. The utilization of DL methodologies in this context facilitates the automated recognition of diverse crucial neurovascular components within temporal bone scan pictures, hence facilitating the application of patient-specific virtual reality otologic surgery. As per the findings of the researchers, it has been observed that DL algorithms exhibit the ability to effectively and precisely recognize segmental intracochlear anatomy [19]. This facilitates the selection of suitable cochlear implant electrodes and personalized cochlear implant programming.

Temporal bones can be produced in a three-dimensional (3D) format by the utilization of high-resolution CT scans of temporal bones, followed by the application of 3D printing technology for further processing. This tool possesses the capability to function as a valuable asset for surgeons to engage in preoperative surgical dissection practice. Moreover, previous studies have provided evidence to support the notion that this instrument can be utilized as a very efficient teaching aid [20].

5.6 Role of AI in rhinology

A diverse range of ML techniques are utilized within the domain of rhinology. One example of a supervised ML system is commonly referred to as “classification.” In this system, the ML algorithm makes predictions regarding the category or class to which an object belongs. When utilized, this technique could distinguish between sinuses that are opacified and sinuses that are not opacified on computed tomography (CT) pictures.

Another ML technique commonly employed is known as “clustering.” The methodology employed involves the utilization of an unsupervised ML algorithm for the purpose of categorizing things that demonstrate commonalities, principally relying on their intrinsic characteristics. Clustering is utilized to discern and automatically classify images obtained from endoscopic sinus surgery. The application of convolutional neural network (CNN) enables the precise identification of the anatomical structures within the nasal cavities, as well as the quantification of sinus opacification [21, 22].

The convolutional neural network, known as ‘Inception,’ excels in reliably classifying the integrity of the osteomeatal complex on CT scans of the paranasal sinuses. This achievement is reflected by an accuracy rate of 85% [23]. The ‘random forest’ model, a relatively new ML approach, has provided evidence that the prediction of baseline olfactory function in individuals with chronic sinusitis can be achieved by considering the levels of mucus cytokine interleukins 5 and 13.

5.7 Role of AI in laryngology

Computational learning methodologies have been utilized in voice recognition software to assist in the identification and assessment of diverse laryngeal disorders. It has been observed that ML classifiers outperform rule-based algorithms in this context [24]. It was almost 100% accurate to diagnose T1a glottis cancers and other vocal cord lesions when speech recognition and videostroboscopy pictures were used with AI tools [25]. Researchers looked into how to make pictures taken with a larynx instantly recognizable. A DL method was used to tell the difference between the different types of laryngeal cancers. A total of 24,667 laryngoscopy pictures were used for the study. These images showed both healthy people and people with vocal cord polyps, vocal cord nodules, leukoplakia, and laryngeal cancer.

A CNN-based predictor was created, and then it was tested with clinical visual assessments (CVAs). Images of the larynx were put into groups using a transfer learning method called the “ResNet 101 model.” The researchers found that the average accuracy rate was 96.24%. When it came to most laryngeal situations, the CNN classifier performed better than the computer-aided vocal analysis method. Despite the large size of this dataset, the current model is not suitable for diagnosing laryngeal papillomas. This was due to the highly unpredictable distribution of these lesions throughout the larynx, which lacks a consistent location for the CNN to effectively concentrate on and accurately categorize the lesion. AI-based diagnostic algorithms play a crucial role in enhancing physicians’ diagnosis accuracy, especially when dealing with early-stage malignancies or precancerous lesions. The purpose of a diagnostic system, which utilizes AI, is to complement rather than substitute the clinical evaluation conducted by a clinician. This technology facilitates expedited decision-making and provides guidance to healthcare professionals in determining the need for additional investigations, such as a biopsy, when presented with a potentially concerning lesion. Telemedicine can also provide advantages to patients residing in rural and remote regions [26].

5.8 Role of AI in head-and-neck oncology

DL networks are now utilized in head and neck cancer to enhance the classification of anatomical features, hence expediting the radiotherapy planning procedure. The utilization of this method can be implemented in order to safeguard crucial structures over the course of radiation therapy [27]. The researchers utilized ML methods in their investigation to predict the occurrence of nodal disease. This was achieved by the analysis of patterns of gene expression in primary oropharyngeal carcinomas in squamous cells that are linked to human papillomavirus (HPV). The researchers utilized a 40-gene profile [28]. The most dependable prognostic indicator in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma is the assessment of HPV status. The researchers in a study used AI methods to build a proteomic signature that can be used to predict whether oral cancer patients will develop lymph node metastases [29]. The investigators at Stanford University did a study wherein they utilized an ML algorithm for training it with the specific goal of visually detecting oropharyngeal tumors. The accomplishment was attained through white light as well as narrow-band imaging methodologies. The principal objective was to establish an automated detection technique for oropharyngeal cancers to enhance early diagnosis [30]. The objective of the research conducted by investigators [31] was to train a neural network to identify nodal metastases and extranodal extension in patients diagnosed with head and neck cancer utilizing preoperative CT imaging.

A novel form of tumor marker, known as “radiomics,” has been developed by the examination of quantitative imaging data. The progress of radiomics is driven by computational innovations that facilitate the examination of extensive amounts of imaging data, encompassing CT, positron emission tomography scans, MRI, and functional imaging research. The field of radiomics has been created as a means of addressing the constraints associated with tumor markers obtained from tissue and blood samples. This is due to the fact that tissue markers obtained from tumor tissue biopsies only capture a limited portion of the tumor at a certain moment in time, and frequently fail to accurately reflect the tumor’s overall biology or any changes in biology that may occur during and after therapy. Radiomics is widely regarded as a highly appropriate methodology for the needs of therapy monitoring and assessing treatment response. Liquid biopsies provide a comprehensive representation of tumor-secreted components, although they do not offer any spatial resolution of the tumor. In the field of radiomics, the characterization of tumor tissue encompasses a comprehensive analysis of various aspects, including conventional radiological features. This entails a thorough examination of the whole 3D information pertaining to the composition, shape, voxel intensity distribution, and texture of the tumor within the occupied volume. Furthermore, radiomics enables the iterative and noninvasive processing of follow-up images. The utilization of radiomics enables the examination of both tumor tissue and healthy tissue, facilitating the prediction of treatment-related adverse effects through the implementation of a specialized resolution. A constraint that arises when utilizing radiomics in the area of the head and neck is the existence of artifacts produced by metallic implants, like dental fillings [32].

The application of AI in conjunction with hyperspectral imaging has been employed to discern between thyroid cancers and normal head and neck tissue. The previously indicated methodology has yielded promising results, with a sensitivity rate of 97%, a specificity rate of 96%, and a total accuracy rate of 96%. This capability allows surgeons to establish more precise margins during surgical excision [33]. The Bethesda method for characterizing thyroid cytopathology provides a clear clinical decision-making framework for lesions classified as Bethesda II (benign) and Bethesda VI (malignant). The Bethesda III‒V classification encompasses indeterminate categories that present a clinical challenge, requiring physicians to consider various treatment alternatives such as repeat fine-needle aspiration cytology, observation, molecular testing, and surgical intervention to achieve a definitive histological diagnosis. The utilization of AI for identifying thyroid cancers via ultrasound pictures and the creation of ML algorithms for analyzing digital cytopathology slides have demonstrated promising progress. The aforementioned improvements possess the capacity to effectively diagnose the existence or nonexistence of thyroid cancer, hence facilitating the prevention of superfluous surgical interventions. ML algorithms play a crucial duty as a supplementary tool in aiding clinicians to decrease the number of uncertain cases.

5.9 Role of AI in augmenting tele-otoscopy

AI is an extensive field dedicated to the creation of computer systems that replicate human intelligence [1]. ML is a specific subset of AI that utilizes algorithms to generate predictions from data, independent of direct instructions from human programmers [34]. Although healthcare providers have the diagnosis, the accuracy of diagnosing otitis media is still quite poor. The research conducted by investigators indicated that the diagnostic precision in differentiating otitis media with effusion, acute otitis media (AOM), and a normal tympanic membrane by filmed pneumatic otoscopy was found to be 50% for pediatricians and 73% for otolaryngologists. The aforementioned issue is of significant concern because of the substantial disease burden associated with otitis media. This condition ranks as the second most prevalent contributor to hearing impairment globally, surpassed solely by age-related hearing loss and other etiologies [35]. It is recommended that primary care physicians adopt a strategy wherein the utilization of otoscopy is restricted to instances where there exists a substantial likelihood of AOM prior to conducting the test. The objective is to mitigate patient discomfort and anxiety, while concurrently lowering the quantity of antibiotic prescriptions [36]. Nevertheless, this methodology fails to tackle the fundamental problem of inadequate diagnostic precision and could potentially result in further undetected diagnoses, exacerbating the diminishing training and expertise necessary for effective otoscopy.

The emergence of AI and ML technologies has shown a significant potential for enhancing both in-person and telemedicine services through the visual diagnosis of ear disorders. Comparable advancements are occurring in various other medical disciplines. An exemplary example pertains to the utilization of ML methodologies for distinguishing among melanoma as well as carcinoma in contrast to benign skin lesions [37]. Substantial advancements have occurred in ophthalmology, enhancing the detection and assessment of several ocular illnesses, including glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity, and related conditions. The use of digital fundus pictures and visual fields has been associated with these advancements [38]. In the field of otolaryngology, there are current efforts being made to enhance the incorporation of ML methodologies within the dental profession. The objective is to enable dentists to effectively identify cases of oral and oropharyngeal carcinomas of squamous cells by the use of these advanced computational methods. This task presents a nontrivial challenge, particularly in light of the fact that a significant proportion of the American adult population, approximately 64.9%, seeks dental care on an annual basis.

The utilization of ML techniques for image categorization necessitates multiple layers of processing due to the intricate nature of clinical images. Consequently, these networks are occasionally designated as CNNs because of their structural resemblance to biological neural networks. CNNs represent a category of DL methodologies. This process involves supplying a specific input, such as an otoscopic image, to the neural network. Subsequently, the network classifies this image into one of multiple categories, such as associating it with a probable illness state. The following studies have utilized examination results, specifically labeled by otolaryngologists, as the “training set” to train CNNs in order to subsequently label new data that is unfamiliar to the algorithm, referred to as the “test set.” The objective is for the network to accurately replicate or potentially surpass the labeling accuracy that can be attained by a human.

Researchers developed a training dataset by combining otoscopic examination images from Google Images and clinically obtained images. Participants meticulously assigned distinct labels to all 1,366 pictures in the training set, categorizing them into one of 14 potential otologic diagnoses. The diagnoses encompassed normal ear conditions, cholesteatoma, AOM, extruded tympanostomy tube (TT), and appropriately positioned TT, among others. The researchers subsequently employed the Google Cloud Vision AutoML system to assess a test set of 89 photos, achieving a diagnosis accuracy of 88.7%. Subsequently, an assessment was conducted to compare the algorithm’s performance with that of healthcare practitioners who specialize in otolaryngology, pediatrics, emergency medicine, and family medicine. The study found that the algorithm achieved an aggregate physician performance of 58.9%, indicating a considerable improvement compared to the performance of the physician group [39]. Prior studies have utilized datasets of varied magnitudes, incorporating various diagnostic classifications, and utilizing a range of underlying computational methodologies. Researchers utilized a training dataset consisting of 10,544 otoendoscopic images, with each image assigned to one of six distinct diagnostic categories. The algorithm devised by the authors attained a mean diagnosis accuracy of 93.67%. However, the study did not include a direct comparison of physician accuracy. Researchers proposed an alternate way utilizing video-otoscopic data obtained from an Android smartphone. The visual data captured by the smartphone application is subsequently communicated to an algorithm hosted on a cloud platform, which subsequently delivers the results to the user of the application. The outcomes can be classified into five particular categories: normal, obstructed by wax or foreign material, otitis media with effusion, AOM, and chronic suppurative otitis media. The system’s accuracy ranges from 81.58% to 86.86%, depending on its unique properties. The authors propose that the utilization of this platform could be particularly advantageous in developing nations, given the widespread and swift integration of smartphone technology on a global scale [40]. Each of these cases illustrates the capability of AI in facilitating the connection between primary and secondary or tertiary healthcare, leading to faster assessment and referral of conditions that go beyond the expertise of general practitioners. This is especially advantageous in areas with restricted access to expert medical practitioners.

There exist some unresolved issues regarding the application of ML technology in the context of automated otoscopic diagnoses, namely within the field of telehealth. Initially, it is important to acquire images of superior quality, ensuring low heterogeneity. The presence of heterogeneity within a dataset has the potential to introduce bias into the algorithm [41]. When an algorithm is exposed to a combination of otomicroscopic and hand-held otoscopic pictures, there is a possibility for bias to emerge, preferring the identification of more severe conditions linked to the otomicroscope modality. Nonetheless, it is crucial to acknowledge that this bias would solely result from the composition of the training set and should be regarded as a mere artifact. Additionally, the inclusion of high-resolution photographs is necessary, and the proficiency and area of expertise of the supplier may impact the precision of the produced results. Lastly, it is worth noting that the algorithms outlined above mostly depend on visual input. Nevertheless, ongoing research is being undertaken to include supplementary attributes, such as intraoperative myringotomy observations, into these algorithms with the aim of augmenting their diagnostic precision. Despite the above-described obstacles, it is unequivocal that AI will profoundly impact otologic care in the forthcoming years, aiming to enhance the timeliness of specialist treatment for patients.

5.10 Operation-based use of otoscopes in the telehealth setting

5.10.1 Guardian-operated

The CellScope, a device developed by CellScope, Inc. located in San Francisco, CA, has been extensively studied and explored. The composition of this device includes a structural component resembling an iPhone cover, a specialized otoscope head designed to facilitate the alignment of the backward-facing camera’s flashlight and an ear speculum. The iPhone has the capability to download and install the CellScope program, which enables users to acquire and store videos.

The study conducted by researchers, involved the participation of parents of 40 patients ranging from 3 months to 17 years of age who sought medical attention at the pediatric otolaryngology clinic. These parents were given a CellScope box along with an instructional video in the English language [42]. The participants received guidance regarding the process of imaging the middle ear; however, they did not receive any additional support or aid from the healthcare professionals. Subsequently, a second-year resident specializing in otolaryngology employed the aforementioned instrument, after which the patient had examination by the attending otolaryngologist, who conducted an assessment via otoscope. Without knowing where the photos came from, an otolaryngologist examined the pictures that the parents and resident doctors had taken. The otolaryngologist evaluated the visibility of anatomy markers and attempted to establish a diagnosis solely on the basis of the provided photographs. The findings of the study revealed a relatively low level of agreement among raters (k = 0.42) when diagnosing based on parent video in comparison to pneumatic otoscopy. Conversely, a high level of agreement (k = 0.71) was observed between resident diagnoses and pneumatic otoscopy. The agreement between resident physician and parent videos in terms of identified landmarks was found to be quite low (k = 0.087). Therefore, the study ultimately determined that the utilization of CellScope by parents for remote otoscopy was deemed unreliable.

Researchers conducted an additional study in Finland to investigate the utilization of CellScope by parents. The study involved a sample of 41 participants, aged between 10 and 34 months, who were randomly assigned to either the direct instruction group or a delayed teaching group [43]. The parents within the teaching group were presented with an explanation regarding the anatomical features of the middle and inner ear, which was afterward followed by an instructional session on the procedure for taking videos utilizing CellScope. In the delayed intervention condition, parents received instructions to use the CellScope equipment for video recording, without any formal training until 1 week later. The study’s findings reveal that the immediate teaching group displayed a 62% rate of videos with superior technical quality, but the delayed instruction group exhibited a much lower rate of 22%. Following the instructional period of 1 week, it was observed that 64% of the movies in the delayed group exhibited satisfactory quality. Following the distribution of instructions to both groups, it was possible to determine the normal functioning of the ear, the existence of otitis media with effusion, or the emergence of AOM in 40% of cases. The research showed that parents need more thorough training to make diagnostic videos better and more useful. The data showed that in both groups, AOM can be confirmed or ruled out in 87% of cases where patients have severe symptoms.

Remote otoscopy can be used for more than just diagnosing AOM. Researchers looked into how CellScope could be used to keep an eye on the insertion of a TT [44]. Twenty-one kids between the ages of 6 months and 15 years old who had bilateral TT implanted were watched for an average of 17 months. Two separate otolaryngologists looked at the videos that the parents took every month. The tubes’ status was assessed by these specialists, who specifically determined whether they were open, extruding, or occluded. The researchers also listened to the records to see if there were any signs of otorrhea, middle ear effusion, granulation tissue, tympanic membrane perforation, or AOM. The first results showed that the CellScope videos and in-office otoscopy were about 80% accurate at finding a tube that was blocked, partially extruded, or completely extruded. Therefore, the results show that CellScope can be used for more than just AOM. The strong link between the usual office method and CellScope shows how well it works for remote tracking of the TT.

5.10.2 Healthcare-provider-operated

A thorough investigation has been carried out into how otoscopes are used by medical professionals. Researchers did a study to see how well CellScope worked as a tool for diagnosing AOM when used by emergency care doctors. The study used a crossover randomized controlled trial design and took place in a single tertiary pediatric emergency room [45]. Two doctors looked over a group of 96 patients, aged 1–4 years. The check was done by doctors using either the CellScope or a regular otoscope. The doctors were randomly given each piece of equipment. The results were compared to those of a binocular exam done by a pediatric otolaryngology expert. The result showed that the doctors’ ratings were more accurate at diagnosing than the visiting pediatric otolaryngologist’s binocular exam. The accuracy was 0.74 for CellScope and 0.69 for a traditional otoscope (p < 0.05).

A cross-sectional study was done in a rural area of Greenland to find out how common AOM is there. Individuals who are not medical experts filmed the ear canal using a Cupris TYM, an otoscope that is easily attached to smartphones. After that, the tapes were sent to otolaryngologists for the examination [46]. Four hundred and eighty video records were made by 84 children between the ages of 1 and 6. After that, the tapes were sent to three otologists, who each did their own evaluations. The job of otolaryngologists was to judge how well the movies showed the tympanic membrane so that AOM could be correctly diagnosed. The results indicate that the average percentage of valuable movies assessed by the three otologists was 18.1%, with a modified interrater agreement coefficient of 0.67. The panel determined that the Cupris gadget offered no significant advantages in this context. Moreover, they underscored the necessity for supplementary training for individuals lacking specific skills to enhance the device’s broader application.

In order to determine the occurrence rate of chronic suppurative otitis media in rural Malawi, researchers employed the use of Dino-Lite, a portable otoscope with a smartphone-compatible external connector, to conduct a structural evaluation of 281 children aged 4–6 years [47]. The data acquired was transmitted to two otolaryngologists located remotely by healthcare staff who do not specialize in this field. When there was suspicion of pathology, the children were directed to a specialized otolaryngology center at the tertiary level. As per the assessment conducted by the independent otolaryngologists, the quality of the images was classified as extraordinary in 15.3% of cases, acceptable in 72.4% of the cases, and insufficient in 3.2% of situations.

5.11 Conclusion

AI is significantly transforming the healthcare sector by improving treatment quality, lowering expenses, and augmenting access to medical services. A significant number of these applications necessitate access to substantial resource centers and environments. Nevertheless, this technology possesses distinctive qualities that enable its utilization even in the most disadvantaged regions, as it assumes the diagnostic responsibilities often performed by healthcare professionals. Nevertheless, AI functions solely as a supplementary tool for healthcare professionals and should not be regarded as a replacement for human medical practitioners. Its primary role is to offer significant assistance to physicians when faced with complex scenarios, relying on patient data to provide valuable suggestions. The acquisition of unparalleled knowledge in the areas of diagnosis, patient care, and treatment outcomes promises a new approach characterized by enhanced quality and efficacy in medical care. AI possesses the capability to revolutionize the field of otorhinolaryngology, indicating a promising outlook for the future.
